newsitem.title: MEXICO: Banco de Mexico net assets fall, reserves rise.
newsitem.headline: Banco de Mexico net assets fall, reserves rise.

text.p: Banco de Mexico said on Tuesday its international reserves rose to $20.547 billion on April 11, compared with $20.51 billion on April 4.
Its net international assets during the same period fell to $10.829 billion from $11.165 billion.
The central bank said the drop of $336 million in net international assets in the same time period was due to:
--Net outflow from trade with the state oil company Pemex worth $282 million.
--The purchase of $50 million from credit institutions, a product of the partial exercising of options on the sale of dollars to the central bank that were issued during the auction of March 31.
--Net sales of foreign currency to the federal government worth $2 million.

--A net loss of $106 million for a combination of factors including changes in the dollar value of non-dollar assets and liabilities held by the bank; net returns on interest rates and from trading of metals and securities; and net deposits in dollar accounts from commercial banks at the central bank.
Banco de Mexico said that during the same period the monetary base fell 979 million pesos due to a fall in the seasonal demand of bills and coins.
In the same period, the government's deposits at the central bank dropped 11.317 billion pesos, chiefly due to the periodic transfer of funds to federal entities.

The central bank neutralized the higher liquidity coming from the drop of government deposits at the central bank via the reception of deposits by financial institutions for up to $12.555 billion pesos.
The following tables detail Banco de Mexico's reserves and net domestic credit. All figures are in billions of pesos, unless otherwise indicated.
April 4 April 11
International Reserves
U.S. Dollars $20.510 bln $20.547 bln
Monetary Base 76,109 75,130
Net International Assets*
U.S. Dollars $11.165 bln $10.829 bln
Net Domestic Credit -12.756 -10.660
*Net International Assets are defined as gross international assets minus central bank liabilities with the IMF and assets of less than a six-month duration from other central banks.
((--Henry Tricks, Mexico City newsroom +525 728-7902))
